edits.definition: A ray is a part of a line that starts at a fixed point, called its initial point or endpoint, and extends endlessly in one direction; the ray starting at A and passing through B is written with an arrowhead above the two letters, and A is always named first. A line segment is the part of a line bounded by two distinct endpoints A and B, containing every point of the line between them; it has a definite, measurable length. Collinear points are three or more points that lie on the same straight line; if no single straight line can pass through all of them, the points are non-collinear.

Two geometric figures are congruent if one can be placed exactly over the other by a sequence of slides, rotations and flips, so that the two coincide point for point; this means every pair of corresponding sides is equal in length and every pair of corresponding angles is equal in measure. Congruence is written with the symbol ≅, and the order of the letters carries the matching: triangle ABC congruent to triangle DEF states that A corresponds to D, B to E and C to F.

For a right circular cylinder of radius r and height h, the curved surface area (CSA) is 2πrh — the area of the rectangle obtained when the curved surface is unrolled. The total surface area (TSA) adds the two circular ends: 2πrh + 2πr², which factors as 2πr(r + h). The cylinder is called right because its axis is perpendicular to the bases, and circular because the two bases are congruent circles.

The mean of ungrouped data is the sum of all observations divided by the number of observations. For grouped data, the mean is found by multiplying each class mark (the midpoint of the class interval) by its frequency, adding all such products, and dividing by the total frequency: mean = Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf, where f is the frequency and x is the class mark of each interval. This direct method weights every class by how often it occurs.

The area of a triangle whose vertices have coordinates A(x₁, y₁), B(x₂, y₂) and C(x₃, y₃) is half of the absolute value of the expression x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂). The formula gives the signed area, so taking the absolute value keeps the measure positive regardless of the order in which the vertices are listed. If the three points are collinear, the expression evaluates to zero, which is how the formula detects collinearity.

The distance between two points P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) in the Cartesian plane is the length of the straight line segment joining them. It is found by constructing a right triangle whose hypotenuse is PQ and applying Pythagoras theorem, giving PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The horizontal and vertical differences between the coordinates form the two perpendicular legs of that triangle.

The distance formula gives the length of the line segment joining two points P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) in the Cartesian plane: PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²), a direct application of Pythagoras theorem. In applications and word problems it is used to find unknown coordinates, to test whether three points are collinear, to classify triangles and quadrilaterals from their side lengths, and to compute real distances between locations placed on a coordinate grid, such as towns on a map.

A linear polynomial in one variable is an algebraic expression of the form ax + b, where a and b are real numbers, a is not zero, and x is the variable. Its graph is always a straight line, which is why it is called linear. In standard form the terms are arranged in descending powers of the variable, so the term containing x to the power 1 comes first and the constant term b follows.

A linear polynomial in one variable is an expression of the form ax + b, where a and b are real numbers and a is not zero. The degree of a linear polynomial is the highest power of the variable, which is always 1. The coefficient a multiplying the variable is called the leading coefficient, while the constant term b is the coefficient of x⁰; identifying these parts correctly is the first step in evaluating, adding or factorising polynomials.

A linear growth or decay relationship occurs when a quantity changes by a constant absolute amount for every unit increase in the independent variable, usually time. It is modelled by the linear equation y = mx + c, where the slope m is the constant rate of change (positive for growth, negative for decay) and c is the initial value of y when x is 0. Graphed, the relationship is a straight line whose steepness shows the rate of change.

A pair of linear equations in two variables is consistent if at least one ordered pair (x, y) satisfies both equations at the same time, and inconsistent if no such pair exists. Comparing the ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂ and c₁/c₂ decides the case: unequal ratios give exactly one solution; all three ratios equal gives infinitely many solutions; the first two equal but the third different gives no solution, so the lines never meet.

The real numbers are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication: for any real numbers a and b, the sum a + b, the difference a − b and the product a × b are again real numbers. Division obeys closure only when the divisor is not zero: for any real a and any b ≠ 0, the quotient a ÷ b is a real number. Division by 0 is undefined, so closure fails exactly there.

The integers are the set consisting of all positive whole numbers, their negative counterparts and zero, written Z = {..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...}. The extension to negative numbers completes the number line on both sides of zero, and it makes subtraction closed: for any integers a and b, the difference a − b is always an integer, a property the whole numbers alone do not have.

An irrational number is a real number that cannot be written as a ratio of two integers p/q with q not zero. Its decimal expansion is therefore non-terminating and non-recurring: however far the division is carried, the digits neither stop nor settle into a repeating block. Familiar examples are √2, √3 and π, and between any two rational numbers, however close, irrational numbers still exist.

A rational number p/q written in lowest terms (q not zero) has a terminating decimal expansion exactly when the prime factorisation of the denominator q contains only the primes 2 and 5, that is, q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ for non-negative integers m and n. In that case the division ends after max(m, n) decimal places; for example, 7/40 terminates because 40 = 2³ × 5.

A rational number in its simplest form p/q (q not zero) has a non-terminating recurring decimal expansion exactly when the denominator q has at least one prime factor other than 2 and 5. Long division of p by q then produces digits that repeat in a fixed cycle called the period; the decimal is written with a bar over the repeating block, as in 0.333... with the 3 repeating, or 1/6 = 0.1666... with the 6 repeating.

The identities (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² hold true for all real values of a and b. Each expresses the square of a binomial as a trinomial whose middle term is twice the product of the two terms — added for the sum, subtracted for the difference. Check with a = 3, b = 2: (3 + 2)² = 25 and 9 + 12 + 4 = 25, so the identity holds.

The algebraic identity (a + b + c)² expands to a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca: the sum of the squares of all three terms plus twice the product of each distinct pair. It holds for all real numbers a, b and c, and is proved either by applying the distributive law twice or by treating (a + b) as a single term x and using (x + c)² with x = a + b.

Factorisation by the common factor method writes an algebraic expression as a product of its greatest common factor (GCF) and the remaining polynomial, reversing the distributive law a(b + c) = ab + ac. The GCF is the largest monomial that divides every term exactly — the largest common numerical factor together with the highest power of each variable present in all the terms. For example, 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3).

Splitting the middle term is a factorisation method for quadratic expressions of the form ax² + bx + c (a not zero). It finds two numbers whose product is a × c and whose sum is b, rewrites the middle term bx using those two numbers, and then factorises by grouping. For x² + 7x + 12 the numbers are 3 and 4 (product 12, sum 7), giving (x + 3)(x + 4).

Algebra tiles are concrete manipulatives, physical or virtual, that represent algebraic terms as geometric shapes: a large square stands for x², a rectangle for x, and a small square for the constant 1. Arranged into rectangles, the tiles model expressions as areas, so expansion and factorisation become visible: the total area of the arrangement is the product, and its side lengths are the two factors.

The circumference of a circle is the perimeter — the total distance around the circle — given by C = 2πr or C = πd, where r is the radius and d is the diameter. Pi (π) is a universal irrational constant equal to the ratio of the circumference to the diameter of every circle, close to 22/7 or 3.14, but its exact value is non-terminating and non-repeating. Measuring a round object's girth and diameter lets you verify the ratio yourself.

An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence of numbers in which every pair of consecutive terms has the same difference. This fixed difference d, called the common difference, is found by subtracting any term from the term that follows it: d = aₙ₊₁ − aₙ. It may be positive, as in 2, 5, 8, ..., negative, as in 10, 7, 4, ..., or zero, as in 5, 5, 5, ...

The nth term of an arithmetic progression is given by aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term, d is the common difference and n is the position of the term, a positive integer. The formula counts the common difference once for every step taken from the first term, so any term can be found directly without listing all the terms before it. In the AP 3, 7, 11, ..., the 10th term is 3 + 9 × 4 = 39.

A geometric progression (GP) is a sequence of numbers in which each term after the first is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a fixed non-zero constant r, called the common ratio. With first term a, the sequence runs a, ar, ar², ar³, ..., and r is found by dividing any term by the one before it. In the sequence 2, 6, 18, 54, ..., the common ratio is 3.

Uniform circular motion is the motion of an object travelling at constant speed along a circular path. Although the speed never changes, the direction of the velocity turns continuously towards the centre, so the motion is accelerated. The acceleration is called centripetal acceleration, of magnitude v²/r (equivalently ω²r) with SI unit m/s², and it is produced by a centripetal force mv²/r (SI unit: newton) supplied, for example, by tension, friction or gravity.

Newton's Second Law of Motion states that the rate of change of momentum of an object is directly proportional to the applied net external force and takes place in the direction of that force. For an object of constant mass this reduces to F = ma, that is, net force equals mass times acceleration. The SI unit of force is the newton (N): 1 N is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².

The Work-Energy Theorem states that the net work done by all the forces acting on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy. In symbols, W(net) = ½mv² − ½mu², where W(net) is the net work in joules (J), m the mass in kilograms, u the initial speed and v the final speed in m/s. Positive net work speeds a body up; negative net work slows it down.

Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses because of its motion, defined as the work needed to accelerate a body of mass m from rest to its present speed v. It is given by KE = ½mv² and measured in joules (J), where 1 J = 1 kg·m²/s². Kinetic energy is a scalar: it depends only on the mass and the speed, never on the direction of motion; doubling the speed multiplies it by four.
